text: This lab closes out the chapter with solved, verified problems, worked the same disciplined way as last lesson: propose from a known recipe, identify the gap, verify numerically, then diagram the result.

Problem 1: reach ket-01 plus ket-10 over root 2 from ket-00. This has the same plus structure as the standard Bell state, but on the basis states where the qubits disagree instead of agree. Starting qubit 2 from 1 instead of 0 — applying X first — should flip the whole pattern. Verifying: X on qubit 2 gives ket-01; H on qubit 1 gives ket-01 plus ket-11 over root 2; CNOT then swaps the ket-10 and ket-11 amplitudes, landing exactly on ket-01 plus ket-10 over root 2 — the specification, confirmed term by term.

Problem 3 asks for the equal-magnitude superposition of all four basis states with signs plus, minus, minus, plus. Every amplitude has the same magnitude, which is the signature of applying H independently to both qubits — no CNOT, no entanglement needed. Starting both qubits from 1 and applying H to each gives exactly 0.5, negative 0.5, negative 0.5, 0.5 — matching the specification with zero entangling gates anywhere in the circuit.

That third problem is a useful contrast with the others: not every target state needs an entangling gate. A state can use all four basis states with a real, nontrivial sign pattern and still be fully separable, and recognizing that a CNOT isn't always necessary is as much a part of circuit design as knowing when it is required.
That closes out quantum circuits and circuit diagrams. Chapter 5 applies everything from this chapter to a real protocol: building the circuit that teleports a qubit's state.
